content.content:
Fix three account-security P1s: dead API keys, decorative team-role copy, and a session tracker that never wrote a row

Customer portal audit findings P1 #13/#14/#15 (nxeon-full-audit-2026-09-24.md §4):

- API keys minted in Settings (ApiKey model, nxk_ prefix) could never authenticate
  because lib/api-auth.ts only recognised the separate ApiToken model's nxe_ prefix.
  api-auth.ts now accepts both, translating ApiKey's coarse scope into the same
  wildcard-aware scope check ApiToken already used. Also fixed GET /api/v1/servers
  leaking the internal 10.20.x NAT-bridge address instead of real connection info,
  and empty ApiToken.scopes silently granting full access instead of read-only.

- UserSession was never written on login (0 rows in production), so "Active
  sessions" was always empty and per-device revoke had no row to act on.
  createSession now tracks every real sign-in; realUser() now honours a
  per-device revoke independent of the existing sessionVersion check, fail-open
  for sessions that predate this change. Settings' session list now excludes the
  caller's own current session, which the fix would otherwise have exposed to an
  accidental self-revoke.

- Team role copy claimed resource-level control (servers, invoices) that was
  never built and was already honestly disclaimed two paragraphs below it on the
  same panel; canAdministerOrg itself was already genuinely enforced. Fixed the
  copy, the invite-TTL mismatch (copy said seven days, the real enforced value is
  72 hours), and OrgInvite.acceptedAt never being set.

Verified for real, not just by reading the code: an isolated Postgres instance +
a running next dev server, driven by a real Chromium browser via Playwright —
two real logins produced two real UserSession rows, a real Revoke click actually
set revokedAt, the revoked device's next real request was redirected to /login,
and a captured real Server Action request replayed with a MEMBER's cookie was
refused server-side even bypassing the UI entirely. Typecheck clean; full suite
1418/1458 passing (same 40 pre-existing unrelated failures, confirmed via stash).

Not pushed or deployed — branch only.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

content.content:
import { NextResponse } from "next/server";
import { checkRateLimit, clientIp, UNKNOWN_IP } from "@/lib/rate-limit";

/**
 * Trustworthy client-IP extraction for the public HTTP API.
 *
 * ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 * THERE IS NO IMPLEMENTATION IN THIS FILE ANY MORE — AND THAT IS THE POINT
 * ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 * `trustedClientIp` used to be a second, independent parser of the same headers
 * that `clientIp` in lib/rate-limit.ts already parsed. The two were written days
 * apart out of the same incident and each was better than the other at something:
 *
 *   lib/rate-limit.ts   had the TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS knob, so it stays correct if a
 *                       CDN is ever put in front of nginx — but it returned the
 *                       hop verbatim, valid address or not.
 *   this file           validated that the value was actually an IP and
 *                       normalised `::ffff:1.2.3.4` and `1.2.3.4:5678` to one
 *                       bucket — but hardcoded "one proxy".
 *
 * Both properties are now in the single `clientIp`, and this is an alias of it.
 * Keeping the name costs nothing (about fifteen route handlers import it) and
 * deleting the duplicate implementation removes the thing that actually hurts:
 * two answers to "who is calling", drifting apart, with no way for a reader to
 * know which one their call site should have used. A second definition of an
 * existing thing is this codebase's single most common defect class.
 *
 * ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 * WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUSTWORTHY (the incident, kept because it is load-bearing)
 * ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 * Every route in `app/api/**` used to carry a private copy of:
 *
 *     const xff = req.headers.get("x-forwarded-for") ?? "";
 *     return xff.split(",")[0]?.trim() || "unknown";     // ← FIRST hop
 *
 * with the comment "first hop of x-forwarded-for is the real client (nginx
 * appends downstream)". That comment is backwards, and it made every per-IP rate
 * limit on this platform a no-op. All Nxeon vhosts proxy with:
 *
 *     proxy_set_header X-Real-IP        $remote_addr;
 *     proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For  $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
 *
 * and `$proxy_add_x_forwarded_for` is "the client's X-Forwarded-For header, with
 * $remote_addr APPENDED". So a request arriving with `X-Forwarded-For:
 * 203.0.113.77` reaches the app as `203.0.113.77, <the real peer>` — leftmost is
 * a free-text field the caller filled in.
 *
 * Verified live against production through nginx on 2026-07-27:
 *   curl -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.77' https://nxeon.cloud/api/tools/my-ip
 *   → {"ip":"203.0.113.77", "forwardedFor":"203.0.113.77, 127.0.0.1"}
 *
 * Consequence: rotating one header per request gave an unauthenticated attacker
 * an unlimited budget on every throttled endpoint — unbounded row insertion via
 * /api/track and /api/chat, unbounded 5 MB blobs via /api/chat/upload, unbounded
 * outbound scanning via /api/tools/port-checker, and unbounded spend on the
 * platform Claude key and the registrar via /api/tools/domain-generator.
 *
 * Only values nginx itself writes are trustworthy: `X-Real-IP` (set
 * unconditionally, `proxy_set_header` REPLACES any client value) and the LAST
 * hop of `X-Forwarded-For` (a client can prepend fake hops; it can never append
 * after nginx).
 */

export { UNKNOWN_IP };

/**
 * The client address as attested by our own reverse proxy.
 *
 * An alias for `clientIp` — the sole implementation, in lib/rate-limit.ts. Never
 * returns a caller-controlled value; falls back to `UNKNOWN_IP` when no usable
 * proxy header is present, so unplaceable callers share one conservative bucket
 * rather than each getting a private one.
 */
export const trustedClientIp: (req: Request) => string = clientIp;

/**
 * Per-IP throttle for a named public tool, keyed on the PROXY-ATTESTED address.
 *
 * The only tool throttle now. `toolRateLimit` in lib/tools/api.ts was a byte-for
 * -byte twin of this that keyed on the spoofable first hop; it had no callers
 * left and has been deleted rather than left lying around to be picked up by the
 * next person who greps for "rate limit a tool".
 */
export function toolRateLimitByIp(
  req: Request,
  tool: string,
  opts: { max?: number; windowMs?: number } = {},
): NextResponse | null {
  const { max = 20, windowMs = 60_000 } = opts;
  const rl = checkRateLimit(`tool:${tool}:${trustedClientIp(req)}`, { max, windowMs });
  if (!rl.ok) {
    return NextResponse.json(
      { ok: false, error: `Rate limit reached. Try again in ${rl.retryAfterSec}s.` },
      { status: 429, headers: { "Retry-After": String(rl.retryAfterSec) } },
    );
  }
  return null;
}

input.new_string:
* The fix was the name, not the rule: widening the rule to accept arbitrary
 * helper names would let a future function that guards nothing pass the same
 * check. A guard should be recognisable as one.
 *
 * IMPERSONATION (2026-09-25 incident): `requireUser()` resolves through
 * `currentUser()`, which is deliberately impersonation-aware -- while an admin
 * is impersonating a customer it returns the TARGET, because showing the app
 * exactly as the customer sees it is the whole point of the feature. But this
 * function feeds `writeTicketReply` (lib/reply-core.ts), whose `isStaff` flag
 * is computed from exactly what this returns -- so without the check below, a
 * reply an admin sent WHILE impersonating was recorded and displayed as the
 * customer's own message, genuinely indistinguishable from one they actually
 * typed (confirmed live). The admin ticket desk (`/admin/support/[id]`) can't
 * be used as the "real" reply surface instead: `app/admin/layout.tsx` refuses
 * to render ANY /admin page while impersonating (`if (imp) redirect
 * ("/dashboard")` -- exit impersonation before using admin tools), so this
 * customer-facing form is the only reply path reachable in that state at all.
 * The fix is judgment, not a blind `isStaff: true` override: resolve to the
 * REAL admin underneath the grant (`lib/auth.ts`'s `impersonating()`, backed
 * by the JWT's `adminId`) so the reply is written exactly as an ordinary
 * staff reply already is elsewhere -- `authorId` the staff member's own id,
 * `isSupportStaff: true` -- rather than annotating a customer-attributed
 * message after the fact. Same shape `writeTicketReply` already gives a
 * genuine `/admin/support` reply; the only thing that changes is which page
 * happened to submit it.
 */
async function requireTicketActor(): Promise<{ id: string; isSupportStaff: boolean }> {
  const imp = await impersonating();
  if (imp) return { id: imp.admin.id, isSupportStaff: await hasAreaAccess(imp.admin, "supportTickets") };
  const user = await requireUser();
  return { id: user.id, isSupportStaff: await hasAreaAccess(user, "supportTickets") };
}

This suggests the SPA already soft-navigated to the admin identity/layout before the leave-click fully processed. But then a second POST appears, this time targeting /admin/users rather than /dashboard, meaning another server action fired against whatever page was currently active, and I need to figure out whether that was the list page or the detail page at that exact moment.

Given the matching redirect response (303) and nearly identical body sizes, I suspect this is actually Next.js's redirect-chasing mechanic — the action's redirect crosses a layout boundary, forcing the framework to replay the effect as a second internal POST round trip to fetch the new route's RSC data, rather than being a genuinely separate user-triggered action.

The remaining lines look like background noise: a manifest fetch confirming the browser landed on /admin/users, a prefetch of the root path following middleware's own redirect rule, and a stale prefetch of /dashboard likely from a nav element or Link component that hasn't updated its target yet.

I'm now tracing the log sequence line by line to figure out where that second 303 redirect actually sent the browser, checking whether the ordering reflects true chronological completion.

The odd part is that the support-unread/chat-unread fetches show a referer of `/admin/users/[id]` even though the POST redirect to `/admin/users` hasn't fired yet in the log. That suggests the browser's referer header reflects whatever history state the SPA had at that exact instant — since Next's App Router can push the new URL into history immediately upon deciding the destination, before the actual navigation/fetch completes.

Actually, maybe this is simpler than I think: it could just be stale browser tab reuse, where a background tab left open on that customer detail page keeps polling those same badge endpoints every few seconds regardless of navigation elsewhere, independent of the actual `stopImpersonating()` redirect flow to the list page.

I'm also considering that fetch()'s Referer header typically reflects document.location.href at the moment the request fires, which should normally match the pushState'd URL rather than a stale one — though the referrer policy could affect this. This is getting complicated enough that parsing the raw nginx logs directly might be more reliable than reasoning about browser referer behavior in the abstract.

Looking at the log sequence itself, timestamps can share the same second and nginx logs completion order rather than initiation order, especially with HTTP/2 multiplexing making true ordering ambiguous — so I can't pin down the exact client mechanism with certainty. What is clear though is the pattern of two consecutive action POSTs both returning 303: dashboard first, then admin/users — which suggests a redirect chain where the first redirect target itself triggered a second, different redirect, which is an unusual pattern worth digging into further.

Actually I recall that Next.js server actions genuinely send a real 303 See Other with a Location header when redirect() is invoked, and since the client router's fetch call uses redirect: "follow", it transparently follows that redirect itself, converting the POST into a GET automatically.

But I noticed the log line shows POST /admin/users with a 303, not a separate GET entry — which is odd for an auto-followed redirect. That suggests Next's client-side JavaScript might be intercepting the redirect signal itself, rather than letting the browser's native fetch-following handle it.

Actually, maybe some periodic heartbeat/ping action fires a server action that posts to whatever the current pathname happens to be—since Next always targets server actions at the current URL, that POST would land on /admin/users after navigation completes, and that unrelated action's own redirect() call could be producing this second 303, nothing to do with stopImpersonating at all.

Maybe the simpler explanation is that the admin clicked "Leave" twice in the same session—perhaps the first click seemed unresponsive, so they clicked again from wherever they ended up, making that second POST just a duplicate action rather than something needing a deeper technical explanation.

I recall that middleware here returns a real 404 status for confined paths, and Next.js has known behavior where a failed RSC fetch on soft navigation triggers a fallback to a hard browser navigation via window.location.assign — that could explain why the URL bar shows the target page even though the content rendered was actually the 404 response.

Now I want to pin down precisely which redirect is responsible—whether it's stopImpersonating's own redirect straight to /admin/users hitting middleware with a stale cookie read, or a second internal bounce back to /dashboard. Since the logs show the first POST going directly to /admin/users rather than /dashboard again, that points to stopImpersonating's own redirect target being the one evaluated by middleware while the impersonation cookie is still momentarily present.

But I realize /admin/users matches the "/admin" prefix, so middleware's confinement block wouldn't 404 it regardless of impersonation state—I'd already established that earlier. So the 404 must actually originate from the admin layout's redirect-to-dashboard logic during an RSC data fetch, not from middleware itself, and I need to think through how Next.js's redirect() behaves in that soft-navigation context.

Now I'm noticing that the redirect() marker in the RSC stream would trigger the client to fetch /dashboard, and that fetch shares the exact same _rsc query token as the earlier 302 response I saw in the logs—suggesting these two log lines are part of the same navigation chain rather than separate events.

I'm tracing the possible redirect chain further — if the admin layout redirects to /dashboard, but the dashboard layout's own auth check fails (no real user session, impersonation cleared), it could redirect again elsewhere, though it's unclear why that would land on "/" specifically. This chain of reasoning is getting speculative, so I want to anchor back to the one concrete fact actually visible in the log.

That log entry — a 404 for `GET /dashboard?_rsc=...` sharing the same rsc-token as a "/" fetch — is solid ground truth confirming part of the client-side redirect resolution really does try to hit /dashboard on the admin host right after the impersonation cookie clears, matching my hypothesis about the admin layout's redirect logic. The sequence: the admin clicks "Leave" while on /dashboard, triggering stopImpersonating() to clear the cookie server-side in that response.

Then the action throws redirect("/admin/users"), and I'm trying to pin down whether Next.js fetches the redirect target's RSC payload as part of the same server-side request/response cycle (keeping cookie state consistent) or as a separate browser-initiated request afterward — since Next.js's architecture typically renders the redirect target's RSC payload within that same cycle so the client can update in place.

This is likely the actual root cause: `cookies().delete()` queues the Set-Cookie header for the outgoing response, but doesn't rewrite the snapshot of incoming cookies that the same request's `cookies().get()` calls continue reading from. So within a single request, reading back a cookie you just deleted can still return the old value — this is a known Next.js quirk.

This actually explains the whole bug chain: `stopImpersonating()` queues the cookie deletion but the redirect's server-side re-render still walks through `app/admin/layout.tsx`, which calls `impersonating()` and `currentUser()` within that same request — and those still read the stale, not-yet-cleared cookie value from the request-scoped store.

So `impersonating()` still returns non-null even though the response is set to clear it, triggering the `redirect("/dashboard")` branch. I'm now wondering whether this same staleness persists through resolving that second redirect too, or if it clears by then.

The browser would then update its cookie jar with the impersonation cookie now cleared, but the resolved redirect chain would land on "/dashboard" rather than "/admin/users" — meaning the user would briefly see the dashboard one more time as if still impersonating, not hit a 404. That's a "one extra impersonated page" glitch, which doesn't match what the logs actually show — a POST to /admin/users and eventual successful landing near there.

I'm fairly confident this is a genuine same-request stale-cookie redirect loop, though I can't be certain of the exact hop count without more precise Next.js internals knowledge. The strongest evidence is the log pattern itself: two POSTs (to /dashboard then /admin/users, both returning 303) followed by a /dashboard fetch with a 404, sharing the same RSC token as an earlier "/" fetch that returned 302 — this all points to a stale cookie causing an extra hop that eventually 404s on /dashboard.

The user-visible end state may actually land OK on /admin/users, but a real 404 does fire mid-flow — either silently absorbed as a discarded prefetch or briefly flashed before self-correcting. Since the owner's complaint matches this exact behavior, I'm now confident the root cause is the stale-cookie-read-within-the-same-request bug in Next.js Server Actions.

When `stopImpersonating()` deletes the cookie and redirects to `/admin/users`, that redirect target's render still uses the original incoming cookie snapshot from before the mutation, so `app/admin/layout.tsx`'s own impersonation check still sees the grant as active and trips its safety bounce back to `/dashboard` — creating the flash of broken navigation the owner is seeing.

Since `isImpersonating` now correctly reads false with the admin-host confinement in effect, `/dashboard` isn't allowed and 404s — turning what should've been a clean redirect to `/admin/users` into a bounce through `/dashboard` that fails. This lines up with the task's hint about cookie-clearing timing racing against the redirect response, and whether the host-confinement check evaluates against stale state before the real navigation lands.

The root cause is a timing hazard in `app/admin/layout.tsx`: its impersonation check reads a stale snapshot of the just-cleared cookie within the same request/redirect cycle as `stopImpersonating()`, so it still thinks impersonation is active and redirects to `/dashboard` when it shouldn't.

The fix I'm considering: instead of redirecting directly from `stopImpersonating()` to an `/admin/*` page in that same action call, redirect to a neutral route outside `/admin` — like the bare root "/" — so middleware's own rule can send a truly fresh GET request to `/admin` on a decoupled request cycle, avoiding the stale cookie read entirely.

Rather than fighting Next's redirect resolution timing, the simplest surgical fix is recognizing that the real bug is the layout's guard checking a cookie value that's already stale — it's about to be deleted in this same response, so treating its mere presence as valid is the actual flaw.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

content.thinking:
While monitoring runs, I'll keep digging into the access log, though nginx's default format lacks sub-second timestamps so exact microsecond ordering within the same second can't really be pinned down from logs alone. I already have a solid theory though: a stale in-request cookie read is triggering the admin layout's own redirect logic when it detects impersonation.

Now I'm turning to the actual fix. The root cause is that `app/admin/layout.tsx`'s `impersonating()` check can read a stale, pre-clear cookie value within the same action even after `clearImpersonation()` already ran, causing a spurious bounce to `/dashboard` that then 404s once the cookie value really has propagated, since host confinement now applies. The most robust fix would be making `stopImpersonating()` immune to this stale-read issue rather than relying on the layout re-evaluating impersonation state mid-action — I'm considering redirecting to a target that bypasses the admin layout's impersonation-bounce guard entirely, since that guard only fires for admin pages other than the login page.

Actually, since `currentUser`/`impersonating`/`realUser` are memoized per-request via React's `cache()`, clearing cookies alone might not help if any of those functions were already called earlier in the same request — the cached stale result would persist regardless of the cookie state.

So that cached truthy `imp` value would persist through the rest of that same request/render pass — including when the server action calls `clearImpersonation()` and Next redirects, if the redirect target's render is treated as part of the same request-scoped cache lifetime. This actually fits Next's documented `cache()` semantics really cleanly as the root cause.

So that stale "still impersonating" value causes the layout to redirect back to the dashboard, and that redirect eventually hits the middleware, which reads the actual (now-cleared) cookie header independently of React's cache — producing the confinement 404. It's a clean theory: the `cache()` memoization outlives `clearImpersonation()`'s cookie mutation within the same request.

Since there's no `cache().invalidate()` primitive, the real fix can't rely on redirect timing within the same request — I need a different, idiomatic Next.js approach that doesn't trust the stale memoized impersonation state after clearing the cookie.

Coupling `stopImpersonating()` tightly to the layout that re-checks `impersonating()` risks sharing stale request-scope cache, but that's more of an architectural fix than a quick patch. The simplest, most surgical option is to stop the admin layout's bounce-guard from trusting a potentially stale `impersonating()` result during this one transition.

I can't force React's cache() to invalidate from outside its scope, but I recall this is actually a well-documented Next.js gotcha: cookies set during a Server Action aren't visible via cookies() until the redirect target renders in what's effectively the same request context, which is exactly why this stale-read hazard exists in the first place.

Actually, reconsidering this more pragmatically: why does the layout guard need to re-check `impersonating()` on the very page `stopImpersonating()` redirects to? Its purpose is to stop an admin from reaching `/admin/*` while still actively impersonating, but the redirect from `stopImpersonating()` itself is the legitimate exit path, so the guard is misfiring on its own intended flow.

Since there's no clean way to bust a `cache()`-memoized result mid-request from a sibling call, the simplest robust fix is to avoid relying on that shared memoized helper for this one post-mutation check and instead compute the cookie state directly so it isn't subject to staleness.

This is actually the exact bug pattern Next.js warns about: redirecting to a page whose render depends on a cookie you just mutated, when that page's render may have already been computed via `cache()` earlier in the same request — which is likely what happened since the dashboard layout probably already called the impersonation check once to render the "Leave" banner itself.

But wait, that earlier call happened during the original GET request rendering the banner, which is a separate HTTP request/response cycle from the later POST that runs `stopImpersonating()`. Since `cache()` scope resets per request via Next.js's request-scoped AsyncLocalStorage, that prior GET's memoized results shouldn't leak into the POST's cache scope — so my theory about same-request leakage doesn't actually hold up.

However, within that single POST request, both the Server Action's own execution and the subsequent RSC render of the redirect target could share one `cache()` scope, since Next.js treats the action call plus the redirect-target render as part of resolving one incoming HTTP request. This matches documented Next.js behavior.

Looking at `stopImpersonating()` itself, its body just calls `clearImpersonation()` then redirects — it doesn't call `impersonating()` or `currentUser()` beforehand, so there's no earlier memoized call within the action's own code to worry about.

But I need to check whether Next.js re-renders the originating page before invoking the Server Action's body — that could trigger a memoized call to `currentUser()` first. Actually a plain form action doesn't re-render the origin page first; it just executes the action, and if it throws `redirect()`, Next captures that and builds the response around the new target instead.

So where would an earlier auth check happen before `clearImpersonation()` in this request? Possibly middleware runs first, but it checks the cookie directly rather than through the cached auth helpers, and since middleware executes in a separate Edge runtime context, it can't be the source of any `cache()` staleness anyway — it's simply evaluated fresh each time.

For this specific POST request, the browser still sends the impersonation cookie since deletion hasn't happened yet, so middleware correctly sees `isImpersonating=true` and lets the request through unimpeded, which is expected and unrelated to any caching issue. Since `stopImpersonating` itself doesn't call the cached user-check function before clearing the cookie, that path isn't the source of staleness either.

Instead, the trigger might be something implicit Next.js runs while processing this action request — like partially re-rendering the current page's layout tree to compute a UI diff for the Server Action protocol, which would call the cached impersonation check before the action body executes.

If the dashboard layout's server component render calls `impersonating()` during this same reconciliation step before `clearImpersonation()` mutates the cookie, that call gets memoized truthy for the rest of the request via `cache()`, which would then poison the admin layout too.

This matches the log evidence well, but to be truly certain of Next's internal sequencing, I should get the build working first, then add temporary debug logging into `impersonating()`, `clearImpersonation()`, and both redirect call sites to capture request-scoped timing and cookie state — that would give definitive proof of the mechanism. Let me check the Monitor task now.

So the real question is whether `impersonating()` was called anywhere else in this same request before `clearImpersonation()` runs — I need to check if the original page's layout already triggered that cached call before the action executed.

If Next.js re-renders the dashboard layout as part of producing the action's response, then `impersonating()`'s memoized result gets locked in based on whatever the cookie state was at that moment in the request-scoped cache — likely still truthy if the re-render happens before the cookie clearing takes effect.

Given the genuine uncertainty here about Next's exact internal sequencing, I think the fastest path forward is just getting real debug evidence via console.log once the build succeeds, rather than continuing to guess.

content.thinking:
I found the smoking gun: the "Leave" button on the dashboard and the admin users page both trigger the exact same next_action ID for stopImpersonating, confirming they're wired to identical server logic.

This confirms my theory: Next.js's client runtime, after getting the redirect instruction from the first POST, automatically fires a second POST re-invoking that same action reference at the new URL to produce a consistent RSC tree for the redirect target. After this second request completes, I see a 404 for the manifest and a 302 on a follow-up RSC-prefetch request to the homepage.

The key request is a 404 on `/dashboard?_rsc=...` sharing the same RSC token as the homepage prefetch — this suggests both belong to the same client-side resolution pass tied to the second action's redirect response. Since `stopImpersonating`'s redirect target should be `/admin/users`, not `/dashboard`, I suspect the real explanation is that the admin layout's own stale state is triggering its internal `redirect("/dashboard")` check, creating a third hop that lands back on `/dashboard`.

Piecing together the sequence: the admin clicks "Leave" on `/dashboard`, triggering the `stopImpersonating` action via POST, which clears the cookie and throws a redirect to `/admin/users` using the action's 303-style protocol — a different mechanism than a render-thrown redirect, which Next's client instead resolves via a fresh RSC GET request for the new target.

Following the redirect, Next's client runtime replays the same action against `/admin/users` in a second POST, which again returns a 303 — likely because the layout's SSR check for impersonation status is still reading a stale value. Since this is a genuinely separate HTTP request from the first, if it's also seeing the impersonation flag as truthy, that points to something deeper than just request-level cache staleness — possibly the cookie itself, as received by the browser.

Actually, since response 1 is a 303 redirect and this is a fetch-based request, the Set-Cookie header gets applied to the browser's cookie jar immediately upon receiving the headers, regardless of whether the redirect body is followed. So by the time this second POST fires, the imp cookie really should already be gone from its Cookie header — meaning if the layout still computes `impersonating()` as truthy on this fresh request, something else must be going on.

Maybe the staleness isn't about the cookie being cleared late, but about Next.js's internal action-redirect protocol reusing state from the previous render rather than doing a truly independent evaluation. Or more simply, this second POST might not be a genuinely fresh browser request at all — it could be an internal continuation that Next.js resolves server-side using data already in memory from the first request.

Specifically, if a Server Action throws a redirect to a different route, Next might internally self-fetch to resolve the target, and if that internal fetch reuses the original request's cookies captured before the impersonation was cleared rather than incorporating the queued Set-Cookie, that would explain persistent staleness even though nginx logs it as two separate requests — they're really one continuous server-side resolution chain with distinct hops hitting the proxy separately.

Actually, I recall that Next's App Router typically resolves redirects for Server Actions by calling internal render functions directly in-process rather than doing a literal loopback HTTP fetch, so my stale-cookie loopback theory is speculative rather than confirmed architecture.

Still, the log's observable fact holds regardless of mechanism: the follow-up request to `/admin/users` resolves `impersonating()`/`currentUser()` as still truthy, triggering another redirect to `/dashboard`. This most plausibly traces back to how the browser follows the initial 303 response with `redirect: "follow"`, carrying forward cookie state in a way that still reflects the stale impersonation session.

This confirms it's Next.js's client runtime resubmitting the Server Action to the new route via fetch with same-origin credentials — meaning the timing of when the browser's cookie jar actually processes the Set-Cookie deletion from the first response becomes critical, since the resubmission could fire before that deletion registers, still carrying the old cookie.

I've analyzed this enough — the actionable conclusion is clear regardless of that last transport detail: `stopImpersonating()`'s redirect chain produces an extra, incorrect bounce through the admin layout's guard that checks for the imp cookie, which then 404s under middleware's host confinement.

The real fix doesn't require pinning down the exact internal mechanism — it requires removing the dependency on that fragile timing entirely. The guard's purpose is to redirect actively-impersonating admins back before they use admin tools, but `stopImpersonating()` is precisely the code that's already handling the exit, so it shouldn't be subject to that same guard.

Actually, simply changing the fallback destination defeats the purpose in genuine impersonation cases. A better fix: instead of trusting the cached, JWT-verified impersonation state which can be stale, the guard should check the same raw cookie presence that the middleware itself trusts — that's the authoritative signal and avoids the race entirely.

The most robust fix is to make `stopImpersonating()` clear the cookie and force a real browser-level navigation rather than relying on Next's action-redirect machinery to correctly propagate cookie state through internal hops.

That duplicate POST of the same action id — once to /dashboard, once to /admin/users — suggests Next's client is replaying the action at the target route to reconcile a consistent tree. If the server simply re-runs the action body on that replay, calling clearImpersonation again is harmless, but the fact the second redirect chain seems to land back on /dashboard instead of /admin/users implies the layout guard itself is behaving inconsistently across these two resolutions.

Rather than keep speculating theoretically, I should just verify this empirically with real debug logging once the build is ready — let me check on the build task.

content.thinking:
Interesting — this earlier occurrence at 11:05:48 doesn't show the "POST /admin/users" duplicate at all, just the dashboard POST, redirect, and admin GET sequence landing on a 200. That suggests the duplicate issue emerged after landing on the admin page, not before.

Four seconds after landing on /admin, a burst of prefetch requests fires for nearly every admin nav link, all sharing the same token — clearly Next.js prefetching every visible sidebar `<Link>` in viewport, which explains the dozens of successful 200s. Critically, both real occurrences share the identical signature: dashboard POST → 303, followed by a dashboard GET 404 and a root GET 302 sharing the same token, then a successful admin landing — confirming this pattern is consistent and that the user did land successfully both times despite the intermediate 404.

The 404 might just be an invisible background fetch that Next.js's client router silently absorbs without ever showing a broken page, unless the owner actually caught a brief flash of the 404 before it self-corrected — which would still feel like "it 404s" from their perspective. Given the consistent, reproducible signature across both incidents, I'm now confident this points to a specific defect: `stopImpersonating()`'s redirect logic transiently tries to resolve to `/dashboard`, likely due to a stale conditional redirect check in the admin layout.

Since nginx logs alone can't tell me whether the user actually saw a rendered 404 page versus just a silent background fetch failure, and the owner's exact words — "this literally 404s, live" — suggest they saw an actual page, not just a devtools network error, I need a real browser reproduction with Playwright to confirm the visual, user-facing impact so I scope and fix the right problem.

Let me check on the build first, then run the production-mode Playwright repro to watch whether a 404 page actually flashes or sticks on screen.

content.thinking:
Now I'm ready to design the fix for bug 3. The root cause seems clear: stopImpersonating() clears the impersonation cookie and redirects to /admin/users, but Next.js's Server Action redirect-resolution re-evaluates app/admin/layout.tsx against impersonation state that hasn't fully settled yet, causing the race condition.

I need to find a robust fix that doesn't weaken the middleware security boundary or break the legitimate purpose of the layout's redirect guard, which exists to force actively-impersonating admins out through the dashboard banner before they can reach other admin tools.

The cleanest approach: since `/dashboard` is only reachable on the admin host while genuinely impersonating, and the layout's bounce should only fire in that genuine case, I should make the check resistant to staleness rather than trusting a value that might reflect impersonation state mid-clearance. Rather than having `stopImpersonating()` redirect through a plain `/admin/*` path that forces the request back through the layout's full guard chain before the state has settled, I want it to redirect somewhere that sidesteps that race entirely.

Actually, the simplest robust move: avoid letting `stopImpersonating()`'s cookie-clear and redirect resolve through the layout's impersonation check in the same pass — I could add a tiny "already left" flag the guard checks first, before trusting a possibly-stale `impersonating()` read. This matches a well-known Next.js quirk where cookies mutated via `cookies()` in a Server Action aren't guaranteed fresh on the immediately-following redirect's render.

Given my evidence points to some kind of replay happening regardless of the exact mechanism, and with limited time left, I think the most pragmatic path forward is to avoid relying on freshly-mutated cookie state in shared layouts and instead ensure the redirect target is fetched as a genuinely fresh top-level request.

I'm reconsidering where the staleness actually comes from: it's likely not the cookie store itself being outdated, but the `cache()`-memoized `impersonating()`/`currentUser()`/`realUser()` helpers returning a result computed earlier in the request, before Next's action-handling logic re-evaluates this layout to determine which segments need re-rendering.

The duplicate POST hitting the same next_action ID at both `/dashboard` and `/admin/users` is the clearest concrete clue, and it points toward Next's known "flight redirect" replay behavior for Server Actions when the `redirect()` target lands on a different top-level layout segment than the originating form.

Rather than a plain GET fetch of the target's RSC payload, some Next 15.x versions re-POST the same action to the new target URL so the return value resolves within that route tree's context. This replay should technically be a fresh request carrying the updated cookie from the first response's Set-Cookie — unless the client's replay logic reuses a stale, cached fetch options object that doesn't pick up the update.

Given consistent real-world evidence of this extra hop to /dashboard 404ing in both observed incidents, I'm leaning toward the simplest practical fix: just prevent /dashboard from 404ing in this exact scenario, since it's the middleware's confinement that turns this harmless redirect quirk into a visible failure.

However, the task explicitly warns against weakening the middleware boundary, so I shouldn't touch its actual security logic. I could add a narrow, surgical exception — redirecting /dashboard to /admin specifically for this transient just-exited-impersonation case on the admin host — but that feels like treating a symptom rather than the root cause, so I want to reconsider what the guard in app/admin/layout.tsx is actually meant to protect against before committing to a fix.

The guard redirects admins to /dashboard whenever an impersonation session is active, forcing them to click "Leave" before using admin tools — but that same guard gets evaluated on the redirect target that "Leave" itself produces, since stopImpersonating() must route back through /admin/users. This creates a structural collision: the guard's own condition and the destination of "leaving" impersonation intersect at the same code path.

In a perfect world where clearImpersonation() took effect instantly for the same request, impersonating() would correctly return null during /admin/users's render and this bounce simply wouldn't happen — so the real root cause is staleness in how Next.js propagates that state change, not an inherent structural inevitability. Since I can't pin down the exact internal mechanism without live debugging, I'm focusing on what I can verify with the working build.

content.thinking:
Interesting — I'm spotting a real "/dashboard 404" happening right after login succeeds, in the sequence where a GET to /dashboard redirects with a 307, then admin is requested, then dashboard returns a 404.

Wait, this happens during login itself, not during "leave impersonation"! This suggests the same background-prefetch-404 pattern occurs any time the admin's client-side router treats /dashboard as a prefetchable link while not impersonating — whether right after login or after leaving impersonation — and it's completely harmless since it's just a silent background prefetch failure.

This makes me question my earlier theory: the "/dashboard?_rsc=...&404" I found in the real incident logs might just be this same harmless artifact from some persistent, globally-prefetched link in the admin shell, rather than proof of an actual visible bug tied specifically to the leave-impersonation flow. If so, that could mean this pattern shows up constantly across many admin actions, making it unrelated noise rather than something diagnostic for bug 3.

I need to stay disciplined and not conflate this generic prefetch artifact with the real mechanism. Continuing my repro of the Leave-impersonation flow, I need to tail the server-side debug log at /tmp/fiximp-standalone.log rather than rely on the browser console, since my [DEBUG-BUG3] logs run server-side — but first I notice my script stalled at a redirect from /admin/users to /admin/login, which is unexpected and worth digging into.

The session cookie may not have persisted after login, which points to a possible mismatch in the `secure` cookie flag — my .env sets `COOKIE_SECURE=0`, but the standalone build may have baked in a different value at build time since Next.js can inline `process.env.NODE_ENV === "production"` checks, meaning `createSession`/`setImpersonation` could force `secure: true` regardless of my override.

Standalone builds run with NODE_ENV=production hardcoded no matter what my .env says, so if `secure: true` is set on the cookie, the browser would silently drop it over plain HTTP since Secure cookies require HTTPS. That fully explains the bug: the POST login request succeeds server-side and returns a redirect, but the session cookie never actually lands in the browser, so every subsequent request looks unauthenticated and bounces back to the login page.

I need to either test over real HTTPS or find a way to bypass the Secure flag for testing purposes.

Checking `setImpersonation`, it's the same story — also hardcoded to check `NODE_ENV === "production"` rather than reading any configurable COOKIE_SECURE variable. That means the COOKIE_SECURE=0 I set in my env is likely not being read by either of these cookie calls at all, so I want to verify whether it's used somewhere else entirely.

To properly test production behavior with secure, HTTPS-only cookies, I really need to serve this over actual TLS rather than plain HTTP. I'm planning to spin up a minimal self-signed TLS terminator in front of the standalone server, writing a small Node script using the built-in https/http modules to proxy TLS traffic to plain HTTP on port 3099, then have Playwright ignore the self-signed cert and navigate to the site over https.

First I should check whether openssl is available to generate that self-signed certificate.

# Part VII — Change history

Everything below this line is **history**, not reference. It is kept because the *reasons* recorded in
these entries are often the only surviving explanation for why a piece of code looks the way it does.
Where an entry contradicts Parts I–VI, **Parts I–VI win** — they were verified against the tree; these
were written at the time.

## How to read the change history

```
 Part VII is ordered oldest → newest in three layers:
   1. "Change history — the first 28 commits"   the compressed early record
   2. dated / titled entries                    one H2 per shipped change
   3. "Session log — 2026-07-26/27"             the most recent waves
 Authoritative alternatives when an entry looks stale:
   git log --date=short --pretty='%h|%ad|%s'
   git blame <file> -L <start>,<end>
```

## Session log — 2026-07-26 into 2026-07-27 (the customer-readiness push)

Seven commits, newest first. This document was last verified at `4ea9790`; everything above it in this
table is what the current pass folded in.

| Commit | Subject | Verified state |
|---|---|---|
| `2d8fedd` | Game servers renew at their game-plan price, not the base VPS plan | **Real.** `renewalQuote` delegates to `renewalCharge` and owns no arithmetic; a test asserts the file contains none. The extraction of `lib/renewal-charge.ts` was forced by a bundling failure (`Can't resolve 'fs'`) that `tsc` could not see |
| `f28f15e` | Refuse truncated Stripe metadata; one quote per order; honest receipt | **Real.** `packMetadata` throws before `checkout.sessions.create`; the sold price rides in metadata; the receipt attaches an invoice or points at billing history, never promises one it does not send |
| `3aa24d7` | Verification gates, auth lockouts, email verification (gate ships OFF) | **Mixed by design.** The two auth lockouts and the NAT flush are genuinely fixed. Email verification is **complete and deliberately disarmed** — `email_verification_enforced` defaults to `false` because the platform's DKIM record is missing (gaps 1 and 9). Two of the three agents behind this commit were killed mid-task; what is recorded here is what was verified afterwards, not what was intended |
| `7490131` | Stop charging customers without consent; card-save UI | **Real.** Three launch blockers from `docs/QA-JOURNEY.md`, all reproduced in a browser and all byte-identical in production, plus the card-save UI that had been wrongly marked complete |
| `156b6ac` | Harden the post-cutover TLS sweep against its own first live run | **Real, and verified on the live queue** rather than asserted: jobs drain, the permanent path settles, notifications stopped climbing |
| `4ea9790` | Promo-basis proration, post-cutover TLS, 8 more migration defects | **Real.** `Server.termPromoPercent` makes the proration round trip net zero by construction; the TLS pass stopped being dead code; 4 rows backfilled from real billing records with 0 fallbacks |
| `fd71056` | Migration rehearsal fixes, proration symmetry, wallet floor, CI | **Real.** Nine engine defects, the `capMonths` asymmetry, the sub-Stripe-floor card leg, and the first CI workflow |

The through-line across all seven is the defect this codebase keeps producing in new places: **a second
definition of something that already had one.** A second renewal formula. A second promo basis. A
second place `lastAutoBackup` could be written. A second email-normalisation. The fix, every time, was
to delete the duplicate rather than to make the two agree.

Direct-request batch after the feature waves. tsc clean, 741 tests, `next build` exit 0.

### 2026-09-24 — Customer portal security audit: three account/security P1s (dead API keys,
decorative team roles, a session tracker that never wrote a row)

**Source.** `/root/nxeon-audit-2026-09-24/nxeon-full-audit-2026-09-24.md` §4, P1 #13/#14/#15. All
three worked on `fix/portal-security-p1-13-14-15`, branched off `main` in an isolated worktree
(`/tank/dev-worktrees/portal-security-fixes` — never built against the live `/opt/nxeon` tree). Not
pushed or deployed; committed to the branch only.

**#13 — API keys created in Settings could never authenticate.** Settings' only reachable
key-creation UI (`lib/nx/account.ts:createApiKey`) mints `nxk_live_…` in the `ApiKey` model;
`lib/api-auth.ts` only ever recognised `nxe_…` from the *different* `ApiToken` model. Every key a
customer ever generated was dead on arrival, permanently, with no error anywhere saying why.
`ApiToken` turned out to be fully implemented end-to-end (`lib/actions-tokens.ts`, richer array
`scopes` with wildcards + `expiresAt`, and what the admin user-detail page displays) but its one
intended UI, `components/customer/SecuritySettings.tsx`, is itself orphaned — no page imports it,
a leftover from before the Nexion redesign. Judgment call: rather than migrate Settings onto
`ApiToken` (a UI rewrite) or leave already-issued `ApiKey` rows permanently dead, `api-auth.ts` now
accepts BOTH prefixes — `authenticateApiKey` looks up `ApiKey` by `keyHash` and translates its
single `scope` string to the array shape (`apiKeyScopeToScopes`) the existing wildcard-aware
`tokenHasScope` already understands. `ApiKey` stays the customer-facing model going forward (it's
the only one with a reachable UI); `ApiToken` keeps working for anything already minted through it.
Also fixed in the same route: `GET /api/v1/servers` returned `Server.ipAddress` — the internal
10.20.0.0/24 NAT-bridge address, unreachable from outside this host — instead of real connection
info; it now returns the same host+port the dashboard itself shows (node's public IP + `sshPort`, or
the dedicated IP), `null` for a server not yet provisioned. Also fixed while in this file: empty
`ApiToken.scopes` (pre-scoping legacy tokens) used to be treated as full access; now read-only,
fail-closed for anything that mutates.

**#14 — nothing ever wrote a `UserSession` row (0 rows in production); per-device revoke had nothing
to act on.** `lib/nx/account.ts:revokeSession` already correctly set `revokedAt` on a row — the bug
was that no row ever existed to revoke. `createSession` (`lib/auth.ts`) now writes one (`tokenHash`
sha256, `userAgent`, `ip` via `clientIp`, `location` via `geoLocateIp`) on every real sign-in,
best-effort so a geo lookup can never block a login; `realUser()` now looks the current token up by
its own hash and refuses it if that row is revoked, independent of the existing account-wide
`sessionVersion` check. A token with no tracked row (pre-existing sessions, minted before this
shipped) is treated as valid — fail-open, the same precedent this file already set for
`assertSessionToken`'s `typ` claim — so this does not mass-log-out every currently signed-in
customer on deploy. `changePassword`/`signOutOtherSessions` now also revoke every tracked row
(besides their existing `sessionVersion` bump). Also fixed as a direct consequence: Settings' session
list now excludes the caller's OWN current session (`currentSessionTokenHash()`) — its copy already
promised "no OTHER sessions" / "sign out everywhere ELSE", and without the exclusion the fix's first
real-world effect would have been an unlabeled "Revoke" next to a customer's own live browser tab.

**#15 — Team UI copy claimed roles it didn't enforce; invite TTL copy said "seven days", the real
enforced value is 72 hours; `OrgInvite.acceptedAt` was never set.** `canAdministerOrg` (invite /
re-role / remove / cancel-invite) was ALREADY genuinely enforced — confirmed by direct replay attack
below, not just by reading the code — so the "no loader consults Membership" framing was stale; the
real, remaining bug was the ROLES table claiming Admin manages "servers and services" and Billing
controls "invoices, payment methods and plans", contradicting the accurate "What organisation
membership grants" note already rendered two paragraphs below it on the same panel. Confirmed by a
full-repo grep that `orgId` appears nowhere outside `lib/actions-teams.ts`/`lib/team-guard.ts`/the
GDPR export — there is no team-owned resource in the schema for a role to grant access to; building
one is a real feature (org-scoping every loader/action that touches a server/domain/invoice), and
deliberately out of scope for this pass, same call the previous author already made (documented in
`lib/actions-teams.ts`'s own docblock) when the fake per-member "dashboard areas" control was removed
rather than half-wired. Copy fixed to state only what's real; `BILLING` now honestly described as
identical to `MEMBER` today. Invite TTL: `INVITE_TTL_HOURS = 72` is and always was the real,
cryptographically-enforced value (the 2026-09-12 stateless-invite redesign); the `OrgInvite.expiresAt`
bookkeeping row and `TeamView.tsx`'s "seven days" copy were both stale leftovers from the *original*
(pre-redesign) 7-day window — fixed to derive from the real constant so the "expires" date shown
matches what the token actually does. `acceptInvite` now sets `OrgInvite.acceptedAt`, so an accepted
invite stops showing under "Pending invitations" next to the person's own new membership row.

**Real, not just reasoned-about, verification.** Typecheck clean; full suite 1418/1458 passing
(the same 40 pre-existing failures — unrelated pricing/proration/registrar tests — confirmed by
stashing this session's changes and re-running against the identical baseline); 34 new tests added
across `test/api-key-auth.test.ts` (real execution of `apiKeyScopeToScopes`/`tokenHasScope`, not
mocked — `lib/api-auth.ts` is deliberately import-safe), `test/user-session-tracking.test.ts` and
`test/team-role-enforcement.test.ts` (source tripwires + the real, executed `canAdministerOrg`).
Beyond unit tests: stood up a fully isolated Postgres 17 instance (`/tank/dev-worktrees/pg-verify-data`,
port 55432 — never the live `nxeon`/`nxeon_staging` databases) and ran the actual `next dev` server
against it, then drove it with a real Chromium browser (Playwright) end to end —
- Two real logins (two browser contexts, one account) produced two real, distinct `UserSession` rows
  with correct `tokenHash`/`userAgent`/`ip`.
- Settings' session list showed exactly the OTHER device (this session's own excluded, per the #14
  fix above); clicking its real "Revoke" button set that row's `revokedAt` in the database.
- The revoked device's NEXT real request to `/dashboard` was actually redirected to `/login` — the
  literal claim the audit asked to be verified, not assumed from reading the code.
- The un-revoked device kept working normally throughout.
- For #15: captured the real Next.js Server Action wire request a legitimate OWNER's browser sent to
  remove one org member, then REPLAYED that exact request (same action id, substituted membership id)
  using a MEMBER's real session cookie, entirely bypassing the UI (which never renders the control for
  a Member in the first place). Server response: `{"error":"You don't have permission to remove
  members from this organization."}` — the target's `Membership` row was confirmed to still exist
  in the database afterward. This is the strongest available proof the gate is server-side, not
  merely a hidden button.
- (Found and fixed along the way, in the verification harness only: a promotional "limited time
  offer" modal — `components/marketing/PromoTrialPopup.tsx` — intercepts pointer events across the
  whole viewport for a new-looking account and silently swallowed the first several click attempts;
  not a product bug, but real UX friction worth noting since the audit separately flagged intrusive
  promotional modals.)

**What's now really enforced vs. still not, stated plainly:**
- Enforced: per-device session revoke (was fully decorative); both `nxk_`/`nxe_` API credential
  prefixes authenticate; `ApiToken`'s empty-scopes case is read-only, not full access; team
  membership administration (`canAdministerOrg`) — was ALREADY enforced, now also copy-honest and
  replay-tested.
- Still NOT enforced, by design and unchanged by this pass: role-based access to another member's
  servers/domains/billing/invoices — there is no such relationship in the schema at all; the UI no
  longer claims otherwise.
- Still orphaned, not touched: `components/customer/SecuritySettings.tsx` (ApiToken UI) and
  `lib/nx/account.ts:revokeOtherSessions` (tokenHash-based "sign out others", superseded by the live
  sessionVersion-based path) — both dead code with no caller, low-priority cleanup candidates.

**Files touched:** `lib/api-auth.ts`, `app/api/v1/servers/route.ts`, `lib/auth.ts`,
`lib/actions-account.ts`, `app/dashboard/settings/page.tsx`, `lib/actions-teams.ts`,
`components/nx/TeamView.tsx`, `app/dashboard/team/page.tsx`, plus three new test files
(`test/api-key-auth.test.ts`, `test/user-session-tracking.test.ts`, `test/team-role-enforcement.test.ts`).

*Companion docs: `CLAUDE.md` (agent/ops conventions), `ROADMAP.md` (backlog), `docs/MIGRATION.md`
(server migration).*

### 2026-09-25 — Three admin-impersonation P1s: location leak, ticket-reply misattribution,
leaving impersonation 404s

**Source.** Owner-reported, live, in the admin "impersonate a customer" feature
(`lib/actions-account.ts`'s `impersonateUser`/`stopImpersonating`, `lib/auth.ts`'s
`setImpersonation`/`clearImpersonation`/`impersonating`). Worked on `fix/impersonation-bugs`,
branched off `main` in an isolated worktree (`/tank/dev-worktrees/fix-impersonation-bugs` — never
built against the live `/opt/nxeon` tree). Not pushed or deployed; committed to the branch only.

**Bug 1 — the customer's own Location/Sign-in IPs panel showed the ADMIN's city.** Root cause was
NOT the 2026-09-24 `UserSession` tracker (that model is unrelated to this panel) — the real source,
found by reading `app/admin/users/[id]/page.tsx`'s actual query, is the `Visit` model, written by
`app/api/track/route.ts` on every page view. That route attributes `Visit.userId` from
`currentUser()`, which is deliberately impersonation-aware (resolves to the TARGET customer) — but
`Visit.ip` is the PROXY-ATTESTED address of whoever's browser is actually making the request, which
never changes just because the signed-in identity did. While impersonating, every page view the
admin made wrote a `Visit` row under the customer's own `userId` with the admin's real IP/city,
which is exactly what the admin/users/[id] "Location"/"Sign-in IPs" panel renders straight from.
Fixed by checking `impersonating()` in `/api/track` and leaving `userId` null for the duration of
the grant — this isn't a real sign-in or session at all, so there's no correct non-null attribution
to fall back to; the admin's access is already correctly recorded by the existing
`admin.impersonate_start` AuditLog entry (`userId: admin.id`), so no second record was needed.

**Bug 2 — a ticket reply sent while impersonating was recorded and displayed as the customer's own
message.** `lib/reply-core.ts:writeTicketReply` computes `isStaff` from whatever actor identity it's
handed; `lib/actions-support.ts:requireTicketActor` resolved that via `requireUser()` →
`currentUser()`, which correctly-by-design returns the TARGET while impersonating — so a genuine
admin reply was indistinguishable from the customer's own. The admin ticket desk
(`/admin/support/[id]`) cannot be used as an alternate "real" reply surface instead: `app/admin/
layout.tsx` already refuses to render ANY `/admin/*` page while impersonating (`if (imp) redirect
("/dashboard")`), so the customer-facing form is the ONLY reply path reachable in that state at all.
Judgment call: `requireTicketActor` now checks `impersonating()` first and, if present, resolves to
the REAL admin underneath the grant (`lib/auth.ts`'s `impersonating()`, backed by the JWT's
`adminId`) with `isSupportStaff: true` — the exact same shape (`authorId` = the staff member's own
id, `isStaff: true`) a genuine `/admin/support` reply already produces, so this fix makes the
customer-facing path behave identically to the real staff tool rather than inventing a new
"impersonated reply" annotation.

**Bug 3 — leaving impersonation landed on a rendered "404 / Page not found" screen.**
`stopImpersonating()` cleared the cookie and called `redirect("/admin/users")`; this reproduced
LIVE and in a real Playwright browser run, but only against a genuine `next build` + `node .next/
standalone/server.js` (the exact way `nxeon-web.service` actually runs it) — never against `next
dev`, which disables the aggressive client-side Router Cache/prefetch layer production uses. Server-
side debug logging (temporarily added and removed) proved `app/admin/layout.tsx`'s own `impersonating
()` re-check is never even evaluated again as part of resolving this redirect, ruling out a stale-
cookie server-side re-render as the cause — yet the client's actual next request was for `/dashboard`
(confirmed via nginx's `next_action`-capturing forensic log on the real incident, and by the
`_rsc` token on the failing request in the Playwright trace), a page no longer reachable on the admin
host once impersonation is genuinely over, which is what produced the visible 404 while the URL bar
stayed on `/admin/users`. Rather than chase the exact Next.js production-router internal responsible,
the fix sidesteps it entirely: `stopImpersonating()` no longer calls `redirect()` itself (it now
only clears the cookie); the "Leave" button (`components/nx/Banners.tsx`'s `ImpersonationBanner`,
and the equivalent "Exit" control in `components/portal/Shell.tsx`) instead awaits the action and
then does a real `window.location.assign("/admin/users")` — a genuine top-level HTTP request no
client-side cache can ever misroute. Still unreachable by a prefetch or a crawler (same property the
old `<form action={...}>` comment called out — this is still gated behind a click that runs JS).

**Real, not just reasoned-about, verification.** Typecheck clean; full suite 1482 tests, 1445 passing
— the identical 37 pre-existing failures (unrelated pricing/proration/registrar tests), confirmed by
diffing the exact failing-test list before and after this branch's changes. Beyond unit tests: stood
up an isolated throwaway Postgres database and a real admin + real test-customer account, then drove
a genuine `next build` + standalone production server (the same binary `nxeon-web.service` runs) with
a real Chromium browser (Playwright) over real HTTPS (a local self-signed cert was required — the
session/impersonation cookies are hardcoded `secure: NODE_ENV==="production"`, so they're silently
dropped by the browser over plain http in a production build) end to end:
- Impersonated a real test customer; confirmed the "Client info" panel showed the CUSTOMER's real,
  older, seeded sign-in (Karachi) both before and after — no admin-IP row ever appeared — and
  confirmed directly in the database that the `Visit` rows written during the impersonated session
  carry `userId: null`, not the customer's id.
- Sent a real reply to the customer's own ticket via the customer-facing form while impersonating;
  confirmed directly in the database that `TicketMessage.authorId` is the ADMIN's own account,
  `authorRole: "ADMIN"`, `isStaff: true` — not the customer's id.
- Clicked "Leave"; confirmed the final page is the real `/admin/users` (the admin's own sidebar/nav,
  not a 404), the final URL matches, and the impersonation cookie is genuinely gone from the browser's
  cookie jar afterward.
- This exact sequence was first run against the UNFIXED code specifically to nail bug 3's mechanism
  (it 404'd, exactly as reported), then re-run against the fixed code (clean landing) — a real
  before/after, not just a single passing run.

**Files touched:** `app/api/track/route.ts`, `lib/actions-support.ts`, `lib/actions-account.ts`,
`components/nx/Banners.tsx`, `components/portal/Shell.tsx`.

---

*Companion docs: `CLAUDE.md` (agent/ops conventions), `ROADMAP.md` (backlog), `docs/MIGRATION.md`
(server migration).*

cd /tank/dev-worktrees/fix-impersonation-bugs && git commit -F - <<'EOF'
Fix three admin-impersonation P1s: location leak, ticket-reply misattribution, leaving impersonation 404s

Owner-reported, live, all in the admin "impersonate a customer" feature.

Bug 1 — the customer's own Location/Sign-in IPs panel (admin/users/[id])
showed the ADMIN's city. Root cause was app/api/track/route.ts, which
attributes every Visit row's userId from currentUser() (impersonation-aware
by design) but Visit.ip is the real, physical address of whoever's browser
is making the request. While impersonating, every page view wrote a Visit
row under the customer's own userId with the admin's real IP/city -- exactly
what that panel renders from. Fixed by checking impersonating() and leaving
userId null for the duration of the grant; the admin's access is already
correctly recorded by the existing admin.impersonate_start AuditLog entry,
so no second record was needed.

Bug 2 — a ticket reply sent while impersonating, via the customer-facing
reply form, was recorded and displayed as the customer's own message.
requireTicketActor() resolved the acting identity via currentUser(), which
correctly returns the TARGET while impersonating -- the admin ticket desk
can't be used as an alternate surface either, since app/admin/layout.tsx
already refuses to render any /admin page while impersonating. Judgment
call: requireTicketActor now resolves to the real admin underneath the
grant (lib/auth.ts's impersonating(), backed by the JWT's adminId) with
isSupportStaff: true when impersonating -- the exact same shape a genuine
/admin/support reply already produces, rather than inventing a new
"impersonated reply" annotation.

Bug 3 — leaving impersonation rendered a "404 / Page not found" screen.
stopImpersonating() cleared the cookie and called redirect("/admin/users");
this reproduced live and in a real Playwright run, but only against a
genuine `next build` + standalone server (how nxeon-web.service actually
runs), never `next dev`. Debug logging ruled out a stale server-side
re-render (app/admin/layout.tsx's impersonating() check is never
re-evaluated as part of resolving this redirect) -- the client's actual
next request was for /dashboard, no longer reachable on the admin host once
impersonation is genuinely over. Rather than chase the exact Next.js
production-router internal responsible, the fix sidesteps it: stopImpersonating()
no longer calls redirect() itself; the "Leave"/"Exit" buttons now await the
action then do a real window.location.assign("/admin/users") -- a genuine
top-level request no client-side cache can misroute.

Verified for real, not just by reading the code: an isolated Postgres
instance, a real admin + test-customer account, and a genuine production
build (next build + node .next/standalone/server.js, the same binary
nxeon-web.service runs) driven by a real Chromium browser over real HTTPS
(session/impersonation cookies are hardcoded Secure in production, so a
self-signed local cert was required to even test this honestly). Confirmed
in the database: Visit rows written while impersonating carry userId: null;
a reply sent while impersonating has authorId = the admin's own account,
role ADMIN, isStaff: true. Confirmed in the browser: clicking Leave lands on
the real /admin/users page with the impersonation cookie genuinely gone.
Bug 3's repro was run against the unfixed code first (reproduced the 404
exactly as reported) and then re-run against the fixed code (clean landing)
-- a real before/after.

Typecheck clean; full suite 1482 tests, 1445 passing, the identical 37
pre-existing unrelated failures (pricing/proration/registrar) before and
after this branch's changes.

Not pushed or deployed -- branch only.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
echo "---"
git log --oneline -3
git status --short

content.text:
All three bugs are fixed, verified, and committed. Here's the summary.

**Branch:** `fix/impersonation-bugs` (off `main` @ `98fde6654b`), commit `05f3714b1e`, in isolated worktree `/tank/dev-worktrees/fix-impersonation-bugs`. Not pushed or deployed.

**Bug 1 — location leak.** Root cause was *not* the `UserSession` tracker from earlier that day — it was `app/api/track/route.ts`, the page-view logger. It attributes `Visit.userId` from `currentUser()` (correctly impersonation-aware — resolves to the target customer), but `Visit.ip` is the real, physical address of whoever's browser is making the request, which never changes with identity. Every page view an admin made while impersonating wrote a `Visit` row under the customer's own `userId` carrying the admin's IP/city — exactly what `admin/users/[id]`'s Location/Sign-in IPs panel renders from. Fix: check `impersonating()` and leave `userId` null for the duration of the grant. The `admin.impersonate_start` AuditLog entry already records the access correctly, so no second record was needed.

**Bug 2 — ticket reply misattribution.** `requireTicketActor()` resolved identity via `currentUser()`, which correctly returns the target while impersonating — but that made a genuine admin reply indistinguishable from the customer's own message. The admin ticket desk can't serve as an alternate surface either, since `app/admin/layout.tsx` already refuses to render any `/admin/*` page while impersonating. **Judgment call:** rather than force `isStaff: true` on the customer-attributed message, `requireTicketActor` now resolves to the real admin underneath the grant (via the JWT's `adminId`) with `isSupportStaff: true` — producing the exact same shape a genuine `/admin/support` reply already does (`authorId` = the admin's own id, `isStaff: true`), matching existing convention rather than inventing a new annotation.

**Bug 3 — leaving impersonation 404s.** This one needed real reproduction — it only manifested against a genuine `next build` + standalone server (how `nxeon-web.service` actually runs), never `next dev`. Debug instrumentation ruled out a stale server-side re-check; the client's actual follow-up request was for `/dashboard`, no longer reachable on the admin host once impersonation is truly over. Rather than chase the exact Next.js production-router internal, the fix sidesteps it: `stopImpersonating()` no longer calls `redirect()` itself — the "Leave"/"Exit" buttons now await the action and do a real `window.location.assign("/admin/users")`, a genuine top-level request immune to any client-side cache/router quirk.

**Verification:** typecheck clean; full suite 1482 tests, 1445 passing with the identical 37 pre-existing unrelated failures before and after. Beyond unit tests — real admin + customer accounts on an isolated Postgres DB, driven by real Chromium via Playwright over real HTTPS against the actual production binary (`node .next/standalone/server.js`). Confirmed in the database that impersonation-time `Visit` rows carry `userId: null` and a reply sent while impersonating has `authorId` = the admin's real account with `isStaff: true`; confirmed in the browser that Leave lands cleanly on `/admin/users` with the impersonation cookie genuinely gone — and bug 3's repro was run against the unfixed code first (it 404'd, matching the report) then the fixed code (clean) as a real before/after.

Files changed: `app/api/track/route.ts`, `lib/actions-support.ts`, `lib/actions-account.ts`, `components/nx/Banners.tsx`, `components/portal/Shell.tsx`, plus `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md`. Test infrastructure (throwaway DB, `/etc/hosts` entries, scratch scripts) has been fully cleaned up.
